head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Result of the game from state (mouse at m, cat at c, t = whose turn: 0 mouse, 1 cat): DRAW, MOUSE or CAT
Game states with a known outcome are propagated backwards
How many moves the player to move has (the cat may not enter node 0)
A state is lost for the mover only when every move leads to a loss
Mouse at 0 → MOUSE wins; mouse and cat on the same node → CAT wins
The states from which one move leads here
Walking the game backwards from known results
pt == 0 and col == MOUSE (or pt == 1 and col == CAT)
The mover can move into a winning state, so the parent has the same result
One more of the mover's moves is known to lose; when none are left, the opponent wins
Mouse at 1, cat at 2, mouse to move
The starting state; unresolved states stay DRAW

p: Small graph `[[1,3],[0],[3],[0,2]]` (edges 0-1, 0-3, 2-3). Start state is (mouse 1, cat 2, mouse to move).

head: Step
What happens
rows: (0, c, any turn) is a MOUSE win for c = 1, 2, 3; (c, c, any turn) is a CAT win
Its parent states come from a mouse move: (1, 2, mouse to move) and (3, 2, mouse to move)
Mouse to move and the colour is MOUSE → the mouse has a winning move, so it is coloured MOUSE immediately

p: For the graph on this page the search ends with the start state still unresolved (neither player can force a win without repeating positions), so it stays DRAW and the answer is 0.

bullets: Time: O(n³) with n nodes: n² positions times two turns, each with up to n moves.

913.takeaway: Cat and Mouse is solved backwards: start from the known wins, push results to earlier states, and whatever never gets decided is a draw.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Maps every element to an odd number
Odd half of the next array
Maps every element to an even number
Even half of the next array
Build up to at least n
[x for x in res if x <= n]
Removes the extra numbers larger than n
Taking a sub-pattern keeps the property

p: If an array is beautiful, then doubling and shifting its values (`2x−1` or `2x`) keeps it beautiful. Putting all odd numbers before all even numbers is safe: for `i < k < j`, the sum `nums[i] + nums[j]` can only equal `2·nums[k]` (an even number) if both ends have the same parity, so they lie in the same half, where the property already holds. Removing numbers larger than n keeps the order and cannot create a bad triple.

bullets: Time: O(n), the array doubles each round.

932.takeaway: Build a beautiful array by doubling: odd images of the previous array, then even images, and drop what exceeds n.

No power and no score left to trade

948.takeaway: Sorted two-pointer greedy: buy score with the cheapest token, sell score for the most expensive token's power, and keep the best score seen.
